newsitem.title: CHINA: Gingrich attends church in Shanghai, says good sign.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich attends church in Shanghai, says good sign.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich attended an Easter service at a church in Shanghai on Sunday and said the opportunity to worship with Chinese Christians was a "good sign".
Earlier, Gingrich's office in Washington issued a statement calling on China's government to "learn to trust the goodness of its own people".
It said the freedom to speak, assemble and worship were essential ingredients of "a creative culture, an industrious people and a thriving society".

Gingrich, who arrived in Beijing on Thursday, attended a Sunday morning service at the Community Church in Shanghai, along with hundreds of Chinese worshippers and many foreigners including Australian Prime Minister John Howard.
"It's a wonderful thing to be in Shanghai celebrating the resurrection of Christ, and a chance to worship with Chinese, Australians and others," he told reporters outside the church.
"I think that's a good sign, we want to encourage that kind of openness. This is a wonderful step in the right direction," he added.
China's Christians have suffered from widespread and determined persecution in the decades since the communists took power in 1949, although controls have relaxed considerably since the early 1980s.

China's constitution guarantees the right of religion, but many Christians who refuse to take part in religious activities under the direct supervision of the Communist authorities continue to face problems.
On Saturday, Gingrich gave a speech to students in Beijing in which he criticised China for a lack of basic freedoms.
"America cannot remain silent about the basic lack of freedom -- speech, religion, assembly, the press -- in China," Gingrich said.
"In the most basic sense, we are simply asking the Chinese government to enforce its own constitution," he said.

Australian Prime Minister Howard also said he was moved by the church service, held on a sunny Sunday morning with an overflowing crowd of Chinese worshippers sitting on the lawns outside. They followed proceedings over a loudspeaker system.
"I thought it was an impressive reminder of the way in which a group of people who have a strong value system can survive extraordinary difficulties," Howard said.
"Hopefully it's a demonstration that there is greater religious tolerance and freedom in this country," he added.
Gingrich's short visit to Shanghai closely followed a one-day stopover in China's financial centre by U.S. Vice-President Al Gore.
Both Washington and Beijing say bilateral ties are gradually improving after hitting a low point in 1996 due to disputes over a wide range of issues including human rights, trade and Taiwan.
Gingrich is to make a brief stop in Taiwan before winding up his Asian tour.
